q: What proof of citizenship must a US citizen crewmember carry on international operations, and is a photocopy acceptable?
a: Each US citizen crewmember must carry a valid US Passport; photocopies are not a valid substitute.

src.quote: Each US Citizen crewmember must carry a valid US Passport (photocopies are not a valid substitute).
src.note: Alien crewmembers must instead carry their Alien Registration Card (green card) and Passport. Passports must be carried on all flights, domestic and international, so reroutes do not remove a crewmember from a flight.

q: Under the CBP Biometric Air Exit program, can crewmembers opt out, and what happens if they do?
a: Yes. Crews may opt out on an individual basis; if a crewmember opts out, the CSA manually verifies that the crewmember's passport name matches the name on the Gen Dec.

src.quote: crews may opt out on an individual basis
src.note: Biometric Air Exit uses facial recognition to validate the identity of individuals leaving the United States. Air carrier use of biometric boarding is mandated, but the opt-out is per-individual.

q: When operating within a foreign country, whose air traffic and airport rules do you follow, and what is the exception?
a: Comply with the air traffic and local airport rules of the country concerned, except where any FAR rule is more restrictive and may be followed without violating that country's rules.

src.quote: comply with the air traffic and local airport rules of the country concerned, except where any rule of the FARs is more restrictive
src.note: Governed by 14 CFR § 91.703 and 14 CFR § 121.11. See the Jeppesen FD Pro application for further guidance.

q: For international altimeter settings, what is set above the Transition Level, including the standard pressure value?
a: STD is set above the Transition Level: 1013.25 hPa / 29.92 in Hg. The appropriate QNH value is set below the Transition Altitude.

src.ref: FOM 18.1.6 — International Altimeter Settings – QNH or QNE
src.quote: STD (1013.25 hPa/29.92 in Hg) above the Transition Level
src.note: Where QFE is given by ATC, the Flight Crew shall request QNH and set it normally. See Jeppesen FD Pro for region-specific guidance.

q: How long does residual disinsection spraying remain active, and when is it applied?
a: Residual spraying remains active for up to eight weeks (56 days), applied during an overnight parking at a remote parking location.

src.quote: aircraft undergo treatment that remains active for up to eight weeks (56 days)
src.note: Once complete, a Certificate of Disinsection is placed in the Comply365 app under Flying > Regulatory & Operating Docs > International Documents > Europe.

q: During pre-departure disinsection spraying, what must the 787 crew do if on board while the cabin is sprayed?
a: On the 787, ensure the entire aircraft is powered down, including disconnected from ground power. (On the Airbus, crews instead turn off the air conditioning packs.)

src.quote: (787) ensure the entire aircraft is powered down including disconnected from ground power
src.note: A short three-second spray is directed at the floor of the cockpit just prior to the spray team exiting. Crews need not remain on board once the aircraft is configured.

q: During disinsection spraying, how long is the saturation period during which lavatory or cargo smoke warnings should be treated as spurious?
a: A 5-minute saturation time is observed; smoke warnings from the start of spraying through completion (including the 5-minute saturation) are treated as spurious, but warnings outside those times follow the associated procedure.

src.quote: A period of 5 minutes must be observed to allow the saturation of insecticide before any doors or vents can be opened
src.note: Smoke detectors in cargo compartments, lavatories, and avionics may detect aerosol particulate and cause spurious smoke or fire alerts during spraying.

q: At which post-arrival disinsection destinations may a passenger with a serious aerosol-aggravated medical condition disembark before disinsection?
a: New Zealand and Tahiti allow passengers who have identified themselves as having a serious medical condition aggravated by an aerosol to disembark before disinsection.

src.quote: New Zealand/Tahiti allows passengers who have identified themselves as having a serious medical condition aggravated by an aerosol to be permitted to disembark before disinsection
src.note: Keep the seat belt sign ON until spraying is complete; the air conditioning packs are turned off during the disinsection process.

q: How does the US Public Health Service define an 'ill person' by temperature threshold?
a: A person with a temperature of 100°F (38°C) or greater that has persisted more than 48 hours (among other listed criteria).

src.ref: FOM 18.1.15 — Death or Illness Reporting – International
src.quote: has a temperature of 100°F (38°C) or greater which has persisted more than 48 hours
src.note: Other criteria include fever with rash, jaundice, persistent cough, difficulty breathing, or persistent diarrhea. Deaths or illness enroute to countries other than the US and Canada are entered on the General Declaration.

q: For flights to Australia, how far in advance of landing must the Captain report an apparent death or ill person on board?
a: At least 30 minutes before landing, the Captain must report the presence of any apparent death or ill person to the Australian authorities.

src.ref: FOM 18.1.15 — Death or Illness Reporting – International
src.quote: report to the Australian authorities the presence on board the aircraft of any apparent death or any ill person among passengers or crew at least 30 minutes before landing
src.note: This is a country-specific requirement distinct from the General Declaration entry used for other foreign destinations.

q: What separation do PBCS tracks (formerly RLatSM) provide laterally and longitudinally?
a: PBCS tracks are separated by half a degree laterally and utilize a longitudinal separation minima as small as 14 nm.

src.ref: FOM 18.1.23 — Performance-Based Communication And Surveillance (PBCS) Tracks
src.quote: fly tracks that are separated by half a degree and utilize a longitudinal separation minima as small as 14 nm
src.note: PBCS tracks were formerly designated Reduced Lateral Separation Minimum (RLatSM) tracks and require authorized aircraft with the required equipment.

q: What are the RCP240 time limits, and what is the primary means of meeting the standard?
a: RCP240 allows 240 seconds overall for a communication transaction for 99.9% of the time, with the transaction completed within 210 seconds for 95% of the time. SATCOM CPDLC is the primary means.

src.quote: Represents the overall time, 240 seconds, allowed for a communication transaction for 99.9% of the time. Additionally, the transaction time must be completed within 210 seconds for 95% of the time. SATCOM CPDLC is the primary means to meet the RCP240 standard.
src.note: By contrast RCP400 allows 400 seconds for 99.9% and 350 seconds for 95%, met by SATCOM CPDLC and SATCOM voice.

q: What are the RSP180 surveillance time limits, and what is the primary means of meeting them?
a: RSP180 allows 180 seconds overall for a surveillance data transaction for 99.9% of the time, completed within 90 seconds for 95% of the time. ADS-C is the primary means.

src.quote: Represents the overall time, 180 seconds, allowed for surveillance data transaction for 99.9% of the time. Additionally, the transaction time must be completed within 90 seconds for 95% of the time. ADS-C is the primary means to meet the RSP180 standard.
src.note: RSP400 by contrast allows 400 seconds for 99.9% and 300 seconds for 95%, met by ADS-C and FMS waypoint position reporting.

q: What equipment/approval items are required to use a PBCS filing code?
a: CPDLC/FANS 1/A+, RNP-4, RCP240, ADS-C, TCAS, and RSP180.

src.quote: CPDLC/FANS 1/A+ RNP-4 RCP240 ADS-C TCAS RSP180
src.note: Aircraft on PBCS tracks must use CPDLC; if unable to log on, notify ATC immediately and expect a route or altitude change. Non-approved aircraft carry Company placard 1207 PBCS TRACKS NOT AUTHORIZED.

q: In A-CDM, what is the Calculated Take-Off Time (CTOT) slot window?
a: The CTOT slot time is a 20-minute window (-5, +15) during which the aircraft must take off to avoid losing its place in the traffic flow.

src.quote: This slot time is actually a 20-minute window (-5, +15) during which the aircraft must takeoff to avoid losing its place in the traffic flow
src.note: CTOT is allocated by NMOC based on airspace congestion and ATS capacity. Related A-CDM times include TOBT (Target Off-Block Time), TSAT (Target Start-Up Approval Time), and TTOT (Target Take-Off Time).
